section.title: Noah and the Ark
section.sectionRationale: This is the account of Noah. Against a corrupt and violent earth, one righteous man is introduced, given a plan of rescue, and drawn into the first covenant in Scripture. The unit runs from the heading, this is the account of Noah, to the closing note of his total obedience, framing the whole preparation for the flood.
section.thesis: In a world ripe for judgment God commits Himself by covenant to rescue, giving Noah an ark of salvation, and Noah answers with complete obedience.
section.frameNote: Four movements: Noah the righteous man in a corrupt world; the command to build the ark; the covenant and the gathering of life; and Noah's exact obedience.

units.label: A righteous man in a corrupt world

verses.text: This is the account of Noah. Noah was a {{righteous|righteous}} man, {{blameless|blameless}} in his generation; Noah walked with God.
And Noah had three sons: Shem, Ham, and Japheth.
Now the earth was corrupt in the sight of God, and full of violence.
And God looked upon the earth and saw that it was corrupt; for all living creatures on the earth had corrupted their ways.

units.label: The command to build the ark

verses.text: Then God said to Noah, “The end of all living creatures has come before Me, because through them the earth is full of violence. Now behold, I will destroy both them and the earth.
Make for yourself an {{ark|ark}} of gopher wood; make rooms in the ark and coat it with {{pitch|pitch}} inside and out.
And this is how you are to build it: The ark is to be 300 cubits long, 50 cubits wide, and 30 cubits high.
You are to make a roof for the ark, finish its walls a cubit from the top, place a door in the side of the ark, and build lower, middle, and upper decks.

units.label: The covenant and the gathering of life

verses.text: And behold, I will bring floodwaters upon the earth to destroy every creature under the heavens that has the breath of life. Everything on the earth will perish.
But I will establish My {{covenant|covenant}} with you, and you will enter the ark, you and your sons and your wife and your sons’ wives with you.
And you are to bring two of every living creature into the ark, male and female, to keep them alive with you.
Two of every kind of bird and animal and crawling creature will come to you to be kept alive.
You are also to take for yourself every kind of food that is eaten and gather it as food for yourselves and for the animals.”
So Noah did everything precisely as God had commanded him.

righteous.gloss: Righteous, just, in the right. Noah is the first person in the Bible called tsaddiq. Hebrews 11:7 explains that he became an heir of the righteousness that comes by faith, so his righteousness is real yet received, not a claim of sinless perfection.

blameless.gloss: Blameless, whole, of integrity; the word later used for sacrificial animals without defect. Noah was blameless in his generation, that is, a man of tested integrity who stood out in a corrupt age, not a man wholly without sin.

ark.gloss: A chest or vessel, a box for floating. The word is used only twice in the Bible, here for Noah's ark and later for the basket that carries baby Moses through the waters. Both are vessels of rescue that bear the chosen through deadly waters into a new life.

pitch.gloss: The tar or bitumen that sealed the ark; the noun is closely tied to the verb kaphar, to cover or make atonement, and to kopher, a ransom price. The covering that keeps the waters of judgment out of the ark quietly pictures the covering that shields God's people from wrath.

covenant.gloss: A covenant, a solemn binding commitment. This is the first time the word appears in Scripture. God establishes His covenant with Noah, binding Himself to rescue; the covenant of grace, God committing to save a people, begins to take visible shape here and runs on to its fulfillment in Christ.

basic.context: The world is corrupt and violent, but one man, Noah, is righteous and walks with God. God tells Noah that judgment is coming and gives him a plan: build a huge boat, an ark, to save his family and the animals. God also promises to make a covenant with Noah. The question is whether Noah will trust and obey.
basic.hermeneutics: This really happened, and it shows God saving through the ark. A key question is what it means that Noah was righteous and blameless. It does not mean he never sinned; the Bible says he was made right by faith. The point is that God graciously provides a way of rescue before the judgment falls.
basic.originalLanguages: Noah is the first man called righteous, tsaddiq, and blameless, tamim, a word later used for spotless sacrifices. He builds an ark, a tebah, the same word used for baby Moses' basket. He seals it with pitch, kopher, a word tied to covering and atonement. And God establishes His covenant, berit, the first covenant in the Bible.
basic.typology: The ark is a picture of salvation: those inside are carried safely through the waters of judgment, as we are carried safely in Christ. The pitch that covers the ark hints at the covering of atonement. And the one door in the ark's side points to Christ, the one door into safety.
basic.christ: The ark that saves through the flood points to Jesus, the true refuge who carries His people safely through judgment. Noah's righteousness by faith is the same righteousness we receive in Christ. And God's covenant to save, begun here, is fulfilled in the new covenant in Jesus' blood.
basic.god: God is just, He will not ignore a world drowning in violence. But He is also gracious, He warns Noah, provides an ark, and binds Himself by covenant to rescue. Judgment and salvation come from the same God, and He commits Himself to save before the storm arrives.
basic.crossReferences: Hebrews 11 says Noah built the ark by faith and became heir of righteousness by faith. 1 Peter 3 links the ark's rescue through water to salvation. John 10 shows Christ as the door. Genesis 6:18 is the Bible's first covenant.
basic.oneStory: In a world ready for judgment, God commits Himself to rescue. He gives Noah an ark and the first covenant of Scripture, and Noah obeys completely. This vessel of salvation and this promise to save press forward through the whole Bible toward Christ, the true ark and the mediator of a better covenant.

context.literary:
Verse 9 opens the third toledot heading of Genesis, after Genesis 2:4 and 5:1, and this 'account of Noah' runs until Genesis 9:29, where Noah's death finally completes the formula left open in Genesis 5:32. The flood narrative that follows is one of the most carefully built in the book. Many readers have traced a mirror structure across Genesis 6:9 to 9:19, with the numbers of days rising and then falling and the whole turning on 'But God remembered Noah,' Genesis 8:1. This passage is the first panel of that structure, the preparation before the storm.

Within these verses the movement is from verdict to provision. Verses 9 to 12 describe two subjects side by side: Noah, righteous and walking with God, and the earth, corrupt and full of violence. The verb 'corrupt' appears three times in verses 11 and 12, and God then uses the same verb for what He will do: 'I will destroy both them and the earth,' verse 13, and floodwaters 'to destroy every creature,' verse 17. The narrator lets the wordplay carry the justice of the judgment. God will destroy what has already destroyed itself.

Verses 13 to 21 are one long divine speech. It moves from announcement, 'The end of all living creatures has come before Me,' to instructions for the ark, to a second announcement, 'I will bring floodwaters,' to the covenant, 'But I will establish My covenant with you,' verse 18, and then to the gathering of animals and food. The words 'But I' in verse 18 are the pivot. The God who destroys is the God who binds Himself to save.

The unit ends with a single line of narrative, verse 22, 'So Noah did everything precisely as God had commanded him.' Noah does not speak once in the whole flood account until Genesis 9:25. His response to God is entirely obedience. The phrase is the formula later used for Moses and Israel completing the tabernacle, Exodus 39:32 and 40:16, and it invites the reader to see the ark and the tabernacle as two structures built exactly to God's word, each a place where life is preserved in the presence of God.
context.historical:
The ark as described is not a ship with a keel and a rudder but a vast chest or barge, built to float rather than to sail. On the BSB footnote's reckoning of a cubit as about 18 inches, it was roughly 450 feet long, 75 feet wide and 45 feet high. Its proportions, six times as long as it is wide and ten times as long as it is high, suit a stable floating hull. The Babylonian flood story in the Gilgamesh epic describes its hero's boat in very different terms, usually understood as a cube.

The ancient flood stories share a common frame with Genesis, a divine decision to send a flood, a warning to one man, a great boat, the saving of animals, and a sacrifice afterward. The differences are theological. In the Mesopotamian stories the flood is sent by quarrelling gods and the hero is warned secretly by one god against the will of the others. In Genesis the one God judges openly, for violence and corruption, and He warns Noah Himself, then binds Himself to Noah by covenant.

'Gopher wood,' verse 14, is an unknown tree, possibly cypress or cedar, as the footnote says. The coating of pitch was bitumen, the natural asphalt found in Mesopotamia and around the Dead Sea, used widely in the ancient world for waterproofing. The same practice lies behind the basket of reeds in which baby Moses was placed, Exodus 2:3, though the words for tar and pitch there are different.

For Israel, the account had a direct bearing. They too were given detailed instructions to build a holy structure, the tabernacle, and told to make it 'according to the pattern I show you,' Exodus 25:9. They too were called to live as a righteous people in a violent world. Prophets later accused Israel of the very sin that brought the flood, a land 'full of violence,' Ezekiel 7:23, and Ezekiel names Noah as a model of righteousness in a doomed land, Ezekiel 14:14.
context.canonical:
Noah's righteousness becomes proverbial. Ezekiel 14:14 and 14:20 list Noah, Daniel and Job as men whose righteousness could deliver only themselves in a land under judgment. Hebrews 11:7 reads Noah's building of the ark as an act of faith that 'condemned the world,' and 2 Peter 2:5 calls him 'a preacher of righteousness,' suggesting that his long years of building were also years of witness.

The covenant introduced in verse 18 is established in Genesis 9:8-17 with Noah, his descendants and every living creature, sealed by the rainbow. Isaiah 54:9-10 takes that oath as a pattern for God's faithfulness to Israel after exile: 'For to Me this is like the days of Noah, when I swore that the waters of Noah would never again cover the earth.' God swears with the same firmness that He will not be angry with His people. The covenant with Noah becomes the foundation for every later covenant, with Abraham, Genesis 17:7, with Israel at Sinai, with David, and the new covenant promised in Jeremiah 31:31-33 and inaugurated in Luke 22:20.

The ark itself is taken up in 1 Peter 3:20-21: 'In the ark a few people, only eight souls, were saved through water. And this water symbolizes the baptism that now saves you also.' Peter reads the flood as a passage through judgment into new life, and he locates the saving power 'through the resurrection of Jesus Christ.' Jesus uses the building of the ark as the backdrop for His warning in Luke 17:26-27, that people were eating and drinking 'up to the day Noah entered the ark.'

The unusual word for the ark, tebah, appears again only in Exodus 2:3-5, for the basket in which Moses is set among the reeds of the Nile. The two stories mirror each other: a vessel coated with pitch, placed on deadly waters, carrying the one through whom God will save His people.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Moses meant Israel to see three things in this passage. First, that God's judgment is not arbitrary. The narrator names the reason twice, corruption and violence, and uses the same verb for the earth's corruption and God's destruction. Judgment is the harvest of what the world has sown.

Second, that God provides salvation before judgment falls, and that He provides it in precise detail. The dimensions, materials, door, decks and food are all specified by God. Noah is not asked to invent a way of escape; he is asked to build what God designs. Israel, who would receive equally precise instructions for the tabernacle and its sacrifices, was meant to see that the way to be kept alive before a holy God is the way God Himself provides.

Third, that the fitting response to God's word is faith that obeys. Noah is introduced with three phrases, righteous, blameless and walking with God, and he closes the passage by doing 'everything precisely as God had commanded him.' Between the two, he says nothing. Moses held up for Israel a man whose life matched the word he had received, and invited them to be that kind of people in their own corrupt generation. Hebrews 11:7 draws the same lesson: Noah, 'warned about things not yet seen, in godly fear built an ark.'
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The instructions in verses 14 to 21 were given to Noah alone, for a single event, and they are not a command for anyone else to build an ark. The flood itself is a unique judgment, and Genesis 9:11 promises it will never be repeated. Readers should not look for a modern ark or treat the dimensions as a pattern for anything else.

What carries over is the shape of Noah's response. The New Testament holds him up as an example of faith, Hebrews 11:7, of righteousness in a corrupt generation, 2 Peter 2:5, and of readiness for coming judgment, Luke 17:26-27. The passage also teaches that obedience is not measured only by the great act but by doing 'everything precisely.' Noah spent years on the work, and faith showed itself in persistence as well as in the first decision. And the ark was built 'to save his family,' Hebrews 11:7; faith in God's warning led him to provide for his household, a pattern the New Testament applies to the care of parents for their children.

debates.question: In what sense was Noah righteous and blameless?

views.label: Righteous by his own godly character
views.case: The text calls Noah righteous and blameless 'in his generation' and says he walked with God, verse 9, and God confirms it: 'I have found you righteous in this generation,' Genesis 7:1. Ezekiel 14:14 ranks him with Daniel and Job. On this view Noah's righteousness is a real moral quality, a life of integrity that stood out against a violent age, and the word 'blameless' is the word used of Job, Job 1:1.

views.label: Righteous by grace received through faith
views.case: Genesis 6:8 says Noah 'found favor' before verse 9 describes his righteousness, so grace comes first in the order of the text. Hebrews 11:7 calls him 'heir of the righteousness that comes by faith,' and Genesis 9:21 shows he was not sinless. On this view his uprightness was the fruit of a relationship begun by God's grace, just as Abraham 'believed the LORD, and it was credited to him as righteousness,' Genesis 15:6.

debates.bearing: The two need not be opposed. Noah was genuinely godly, and his godliness was itself the fruit of grace received by faith. The New Testament holds both together, as James 2:22 says of Abraham: 'his faith was working with his actions.'

debates.question: Is the covenant of verse 18 new, or the confirming of an earlier commitment?

views.label: A new covenant, the first in Scripture
views.case: This is the first appearance of the word berit, and God speaks of it as something He will do, 'I will establish My covenant with you.' It is then established in Genesis 9:8-17 with its own promise and sign. On this view the covenant with Noah is a fresh arrangement made in view of the flood, God's commitment to preserve life through the judgment and after it.

views.label: The confirming of God's commitment to creation
views.case: The verb used, heqim, 'establish' or 'uphold,' is not the usual verb for making a new covenant, which is karat, to cut. Heqim is used in Deuteronomy 8:18 for God confirming a covenant already sworn. The content of Genesis 9 also restates the commands of creation, 'Be fruitful and multiply and fill the earth,' Genesis 9:1 and 1:28. On this view God is upholding a commitment already implied in creation, which is why the covenant embraces 'every living creature.'

debates.bearing: Whichever is right, the covenant is God's initiative, it guarantees the survival of creation, and it provides the stable world in which the later covenants with Abraham, Israel and David unfold. The emphasis in verse 18 is on 'My covenant,' a promise God owns and keeps.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 9 stacks three descriptions of Noah. He is tsaddiq, 'righteous,' the first time the word is used of anyone in Scripture. The root describes conformity to a standard, in this case the standard of God's own character and will. He is tamim, 'blameless,' from a root meaning complete or whole. The word does not mean sinless; it describes integrity, a life without moral holes. It is used of Job, Job 1:1, of the one who 'walks with integrity,' Psalm 15:2, and of what God asks of Abram, 'be blameless,' Genesis 17:1. It is also the word for the unblemished animals required in sacrifice, Exodus 12:5 and Leviticus 1:3. And he 'walked with God,' the same reflexive form of halak used of Enoch in Genesis 5:22. The phrase 'in his generation' is plural in Hebrew, 'in his generations,' which may stress that his integrity held through the whole long span of his life among successive generations.

Verses 11 to 13 turn on the verb shachat, to ruin, spoil or corrupt. The earth 'was corrupt' and all flesh 'had corrupted their ways,' and then God says, 'I will destroy them,' using the same verb, and again in verse 17. English has to use two words, corrupt and destroy, where Hebrew uses one. Alongside it stands chamas, 'violence,' a word for brutal wrongdoing, bloodshed and oppression. It is the word Nineveh's king uses, 'turn from... the violence in his hands,' Jonah 3:8, and the word Habakkuk cries out, 'Violence!' Habakkuk 1:2.

The ark is a tebah, a word used in the Bible only for Noah's ark and for the papyrus basket of Moses, Exodus 2:3 and 2:5. It is not the ordinary word for a ship. Both vessels are waterproofed, both carry a chosen life across water that means death, and neither has any means of steering. The one inside is entirely in God's hands.

Verse 14 contains a wordplay that English cannot keep: 'coat it with pitch' is literally 'cover it with covering,' the verb kaphar and the noun kopher. The noun kopher elsewhere means 'ransom,' the price paid to save a life, as in Exodus 30:12, 'each man must pay the LORD a ransom for his life,' and Exodus 21:30. The verb kaphar in its intensive form becomes the regular word for 'make atonement,' Leviticus 17:11. The basic meaning here is simply waterproofing, and the sense of atonement should not be forced into this verse, but the overlap of vocabulary is real. The 'rooms' of the ark are qinnim, the ordinary word for birds' nests, a homely picture of compartments.

In verse 17 God says, literally, 'And I, behold, I am bringing the flood.' The emphatic pronoun makes clear that this is no accident of nature. The word for the flood, mabbul, is a special term used for this event; Psalm 29:10 uses it when it says 'The LORD sits enthroned over the flood.'

Verse 18 introduces berit, 'covenant,' with the verb heqim, 'establish,' the causative of 'stand up.' God will cause His covenant to stand. The same verb is used when the covenant is ratified in Genesis 9:9, 9:11 and 9:17, and for the covenant with Abraham, Genesis 17:7. The possessive matters: it is 'My covenant,' belonging to God before it is shared with Noah.

Finally, the 'kinds' of verse 20 use min, the word from the creation account, where God made living things 'according to their kinds,' Genesis 1:21 and 1:24. The ark carries a sample of the whole created order, sorted by God's own categories, into the new world.

typology.type: The ark bearing Noah through the flood, Genesis 6:14-18
typology.fulfillment: The ark is the place God provides where life survives judgment. Peter makes the link explicit: 'In the ark a few people, only eight souls, were saved through water. And this water symbolizes the baptism that now saves you also,' 1 Peter 3:20-21. The correspondence is refuge in a God-given place; the escalation is that believers are not merely inside a vessel but united to a Person, 'in Christ,' 2 Corinthians 5:17, and saved 'through the resurrection of Jesus Christ.' The type falls short because the ark preserved bodies for a new start in the same fallen world; Christ brings His people into a new creation.

typology.type: Noah, the righteous man through whom his household is saved, Genesis 6:9 and 6:18
typology.fulfillment: The covenant is made with Noah, and his wife, sons and daughters-in-law are saved because they are with him. Hebrews 11:7 says he built the ark 'to save his family.' Christ is the greater righteous man through whom a household is saved, and Hebrews 3:6 says 'we are His house.' The escalation is that Noah's righteousness was received by grace and marred by sin, Genesis 9:21, while Christ's righteousness is His own and perfect, 2 Corinthians 5:21. Noah could save only those of his own family; Christ saves people from every nation who are joined to Him by faith.

typology.type: The pitch covering the ark, Genesis 6:14
typology.fulfillment: The ark was covered with a covering, kaphar and kopher, so that the waters of judgment could not come in. The same vocabulary is used for ransom and for atonement, Exodus 30:12 and Leviticus 17:11. The New Testament never cites this verse, so this is at most an echo, not a declared type. Yet the picture fits the gospel: what keeps believers safe in the day of judgment is not their own strength but a covering God provides. In Christ the covering becomes a ransom, 'the precious blood of Christ, a lamb without blemish or spot,' 1 Peter 1:19, not a coating on wood.

typology.type: The single door in the ark's side, Genesis 6:16
typology.fulfillment: The ark had one door, and all who were saved went in through it. Jesus says, 'I am the gate. If anyone enters through Me, he will be saved,' John 10:9, and Peter preaches that 'there is no other name under heaven given to men by which we must be saved,' Acts 4:12. The correspondence is a single way in; the escalation is that the door is now a Person who welcomes rather than merely an opening in a wall. The type is a picture, not a proof, since John 10 draws on the image of a sheepfold rather than the ark itself.

study.christ:
The passage leads to Christ first through Noah's righteousness. Noah is the first person Scripture calls righteous, and the chapter's order is that grace came first, Genesis 6:8, then the description of his life, verse 9. Hebrews 11:7 names what he inherited: 'the righteousness that comes by faith.' That is the righteousness the gospel offers. Paul says God made Christ, who knew no sin, 'to be sin on our behalf, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God,' 2 Corinthians 5:21. Noah's righteousness was a gift received; in Christ the righteousness itself is given.

It leads to Christ through the ark. The ark is the only place of safety when judgment falls, and those inside are carried through the very waters that destroy the world outside. Peter reads it as a picture of baptism, 1 Peter 3:20-21, but he is careful to say that the saving power is not the water but 'the resurrection of Jesus Christ.' Baptism marks a person as having passed with Christ through death into new life. The ark is the vessel; Christ is the reality it points to, the one in whom believers are hidden when judgment comes.

It leads to Christ through covenant. Verse 18 is the Bible's first 'covenant,' and it is spoken in the same breath as the announcement of judgment: 'I will bring floodwaters... But I will establish My covenant with you.' The New Testament shows the same pairing at the Last Supper. On the night before the judgment of the cross, Jesus takes the cup and says, 'This cup is the new covenant in My blood,' Luke 22:20. Hebrews 8:6 says the covenant He mediates is better and 'is founded on better promises.' The covenant with Noah guaranteed that the world would continue; the new covenant guarantees that believers will be forgiven and made new.

It leads to Christ through obedience. Noah did 'everything precisely as God had commanded him.' Jesus is the perfectly obedient Son who says, 'I have come to do Your will, O God,' Hebrews 10:7, and at the end of His life, 'I have glorified You on earth by accomplishing the work You gave Me to do,' John 17:4. Paul says He 'became obedient to death, even death on a cross,' Philippians 2:8. Noah's obedience built the ark that saved his family. Christ's obedience is itself the ground of His people's salvation.

It leads to Christ through Jesus' own warning. In Luke 17:26-27 Jesus uses the years of building as the backdrop to the day of His return. The world watched the ark rising and went on eating and marrying. The warning is that God's patience, which gave the world time while the ark was built, 1 Peter 3:20, is a time to enter, not a sign that judgment will never come.

A caution: the details of the ark, its decks, measurements and nests, are not coded messages about Jesus. The ark leads to Christ because Scripture itself uses it as a picture of salvation through judgment, not because every plank carries meaning.
study.god:
The passage shows God as the Judge who sees truly. 'God looked upon the earth and saw that it was corrupt,' verse 12, echoes the moment in Genesis 1:31 when God looked on all He had made and saw that it was very good. The same eyes that approved creation now see its ruin. God's judgment is not based on rumour or anger but on accurate sight, which is why Abraham can later ask, 'Will not the Judge of all the earth do what is right?' Genesis 18:25.

It shows that His judgment is fitting. The wordplay on corrupt and destroy in verses 11 to 17 says that God's act of destruction corresponds to the world's own self-destruction. He gives over to ruin what has chosen ruin. Violence has filled the earth, and God's verdict is that the earth cannot continue in that state. Judgment is the moral order of creation asserting itself under God's hand.

It shows God as the One who takes the initiative in salvation. Noah does not ask for rescue. God comes to him, reveals what He is about to do, and designs the means of escape down to the last cubit. The ark is not Noah's idea. That pattern runs through the whole Bible: the God who judges is also the God who provides the way through judgment, from the ark to the Passover lamb to the cross.

It shows God as a covenant-making God. Verse 18 is the first time God binds Himself by covenant, and He does it at the very point where He has announced the end of all flesh. He says 'My covenant,' making clear that the arrangement is His, that He sets its terms and He guarantees its fulfilment. The later history of covenants, with Abraham, Israel and David, grows out of this first commitment, and Hebrews 6:17-18 says God confirmed His promise with an oath so that 'by two unchangeable things in which it is impossible for God to lie' His people might be strongly encouraged.

It shows God as the preserver of His creation. He does not only save Noah's family; He commands that two of every kind of animal be brought in 'to keep them alive,' verses 19 and 20, and provides food for them, verse 21. God's care extends to birds and crawling creatures. The judgment is total, but it is not the end of God's interest in the world He made. He intends to begin again with the same creation, not to abandon it.

And it shows God as One who is pleased by faith that obeys. The passage ends not with God's words but with Noah's response, and Hebrews 11:6 reminds us that 'without faith it is impossible to please God.'

For worship, the passage invites both reverence and confidence. Reverence, because God sees the violence of the world and will judge it. Confidence, because the same God has bound Himself by covenant to save, and has provided the way in.

crossReferences.note: Enoch is the only other person in Genesis said to have walked with God, using the same reflexive verb form as Genesis 6:9. Enoch was taken from the world without dying; Noah is carried through the world's judgment. Both show that fellowship with God is the way of life in a world under death.

The only other use of the word tebah. Moses' mother coats a papyrus basket with tar and pitch and places her son on the Nile. As with Noah, a waterproofed vessel carries the one through whom God will save His people across waters that mean death.

The tabernacle is completed and 'the Israelites did everything just as the LORD had commanded Moses.' The phrase echoes Genesis 6:22. Both the ark and the tabernacle are built exactly to God's specifications, and both are structures where life is preserved in the presence of a holy God.

God tells Ezekiel that even if Noah, Daniel and Job were in a land under judgment, their righteousness could deliver only themselves. Noah is remembered as a model of righteousness, but the verse also teaches that no human righteousness can rescue a whole guilty people.

Noah, 'warned about things not yet seen, in godly fear built an ark to save his family.' Hebrews reads the construction of Genesis 6:14-22 as an act of faith, a costly obedience to a word about the future, and it says that by that faith he condemned the world and inherited righteousness.

Peter says eight people were saved through water in the ark, and that this water symbolizes baptism. He adds that baptism saves not by washing the body but as a pledge toward God, through the resurrection of Jesus. The ark of Genesis 6 is read as the first picture of passing through judgment into new life.

Peter calls Noah 'a preacher of righteousness' and says God preserved him while bringing the flood on the ungodly. Genesis 6 records no sermon, but the years spent building the ark in view of a corrupt world were themselves a witness, and Peter uses the rescue as proof that God knows how to rescue the godly.

The covenant God promised in Genesis 6:18 is established after the flood, with Noah, his descendants and every living creature, and sealed by the rainbow. God promises never again to destroy the earth by flood. What was announced before the storm is ratified after it.

God tells exiled Israel that His oath to them is like His oath in the days of Noah. As He swore the waters would never again cover the earth, so He swears not to be angry with them. The covenant of Genesis 6:18 and 9:11 becomes the model of an unbreakable promise of peace.

Jesus says the days of the Son of Man will be like the days of Noah, when people ate, drank and married until the day Noah entered the ark. The time of building in Genesis 6 was a time of warning that went unheeded, and Jesus calls His hearers to readiness.

At the Last Supper Jesus calls the cup 'the new covenant in My blood.' The first covenant in Scripture was announced to Noah alongside the judgment of the flood; the new covenant is sealed on the eve of the judgment Christ bears at the cross, so that His people will be spared.

Each Israelite counted in the census must pay 'a ransom for his life,' using kopher, the same noun as the pitch of Genesis 6:14. The overlap of vocabulary does not make the ark's coating an atonement, but it shows how Hebrew links covering and ransom, a link the New Testament fills with Christ's blood.

study.oneStory:
Genesis 6:9-22 answers the question left hanging at the end of Genesis 6:8. God has resolved to blot out humanity, but Noah has found favour. How will God keep His purpose for creation and His promise of the woman's seed when He judges the whole earth? The answer is an ark and a covenant.

The passage draws on creation throughout. God 'looked upon the earth and saw,' as He did in Genesis 1:31, but now He sees corruption. The animals are gathered 'according to their kinds,' the language of Genesis 1. The ark carries a remnant of every created thing, and after the flood God will repeat the creation command, 'Be fruitful and multiply and fill the earth,' Genesis 9:1. The flood is judgment, but it is also a new beginning, with Noah as a second Adam at the head of a renewed humanity.

The passage also carries forward the fall. The violence that filled the earth began with Cain's murder of Abel, Genesis 4:8, and Lamech's boast, Genesis 4:23-24. The corruption of all flesh is the full growth of the seed sown in Genesis 3. The flood will not remove it. After the waters recede God will say again that 'every inclination of his heart is evil from his youth,' Genesis 8:21, and Noah himself will fall, Genesis 9:21. The ark saves Noah, but it cannot change the human heart.

That is why the covenant matters so much. God binds Himself to preserve the world so that His plan of redemption has time and space to unfold. From Noah's son Shem comes Abraham, Genesis 11:10-26, and to Abraham God gives a covenant of blessing for all nations. From Abraham comes Israel, the tabernacle built exactly as commanded, and the covenant at Sinai. From Israel comes David and the promise of a king. And all of them come to rest in Jesus, the righteous one, the true ark, the mediator of the new covenant sealed in His blood.

The story ends where the flood points. Peter says the present heavens and earth are reserved for a final judgment, 2 Peter 3:7, and that God's people look for 'a new heaven and a new earth, where righteousness dwells,' 2 Peter 3:13. The ark carried eight people from one world into another. In Christ, God will carry a multitude that no one can count through the final judgment into a creation that will never again be corrupted, where violence will no longer be heard and God will dwell with His people for ever.

quiz.q: How is Noah described against the world around him?

options.text: As a righteous man, blameless in his generation, who walked with God in a corrupt and violent world.
options.note: Noah's integrity stands out sharply against the surrounding corruption.

options.text: As the strongest and wealthiest man of his age.
options.note: The text highlights his righteousness and walk with God, not strength or wealth.

options.text: As no different from anyone else of his time.
options.note: The whole point is that Noah stood apart from a corrupt generation.

options.text: As a man who had never done anything wrong in his life.
options.note: Blameless means integrity, not sinless perfection; Noah later sins, and his righteousness is by faith.

quiz.q: What is significant about God establishing His covenant with Noah?

options.text: It is the first covenant in the Bible, God binding Himself by promise to rescue.
options.note: The word covenant appears here for the first time in Scripture.

options.text: It was a deal in which Noah earned his rescue by good works.
options.note: The covenant is God's gracious commitment, not payment for Noah's works.

options.text: It was only a private feeling with no real promise.
options.note: A covenant is a solemn binding commitment, not a vague feeling.

options.text: It cancelled the coming judgment entirely.
options.note: The judgment still comes; the covenant secures Noah's rescue through it.

quiz.q: How does the ark point to Christ?

options.text: It carries those inside safely through the waters of judgment, as Christ carries His people through judgment.
options.note: 1 Peter 3 links the ark's rescue to salvation in Christ.

options.text: It shows that good engineering can save us from anything.
options.note: The ark's meaning is theological rescue, not a lesson in engineering.

options.text: It teaches that only large families are saved.
options.note: The ark pictures salvation for those God brings in, not a rule about family size.

options.text: The ark has no link to Christ.
options.note: The New Testament reads the ark as a pattern of salvation in Christ.

quiz.q: What does the word for the pitch that sealed the ark hint at?

options.text: It shares a root with the word for atonement, hinting at a covering that shields from wrath.
options.note: Kopher, pitch, is tied to kaphar, to cover or atone.

options.text: It simply shows Noah was a skilled builder.
options.note: Skill is involved, but the word carries the deeper note of covering and atonement.

options.text: It means the ark was decorated beautifully.
options.note: The pitch was a waterproof seal, not decoration, and points to covering.

options.text: It has no deeper meaning at all.
options.note: The word's link to atonement gives it real theological weight.

quiz.q: How does Noah respond to God's instructions?

options.text: He did everything precisely as God had commanded him.
options.note: Noah's complete obedience is the closing note of the passage.

options.text: He obeyed only the parts that seemed reasonable to him.
options.note: The text stresses that he did everything, not just the convenient parts.

options.text: He argued with God about the plan first.
options.note: There is no argument recorded; Noah simply obeyed.

options.text: He delayed for years before starting.
options.note: The passage presents his obedience as full and faithful.

questions: Noah was called to live righteously while the whole world around him was corrupt. Where is God asking you to walk differently from the people and pressures around you right now?
God provided one ark, one way of rescue, before the judgment came. How does it comfort you to know that God provides the way of salvation rather than leaving us to save ourselves?
The passage says Noah did everything precisely as God commanded, even a huge task with no visible flood yet in sight. Where is God asking you to obey before you can see the reason why?
God bound Himself by covenant to rescue Noah. How does resting on God's promises, rather than your own performance, change the way you face an uncertain future?
The ark had a single door, and Jesus says He is the door to salvation. Have you entered that door yourself, and who around you still needs to hear the way in?

translationNotes.note: Gopher wood names an unknown timber, possibly cypress or cedar; the word for the pitch used to coat it is closely related to the Hebrew word for atonement, a link many see as more than coincidental.

Blameless in his generation renders a word meaning whole or of integrity, later used of unblemished sacrifices; it marks moral integrity and standing out in a corrupt age rather than sinless perfection.
